claim: EOGT transfers O-GlcNAc to a consensus site in epidermal growth factor-like (EGF) repeats of secreted and membrane proteins, including Notch receptors.
source: The glycosyltransferase EOGT transfers O-GlcNAc to a consensus site in epidermal growth factor-like (EGF) repeats of a limited number of secreted and membrane proteins, including Notch receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: In EOGT-deficient cells, the binding of DLL1 and DLL4 was reduced.
source: In EOGT-deficient cells, the binding of DLL1 and DLL4, but not JAG1, canonical Notch ligands was reduced, and ligand-induced Notch signaling was impaired.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry and bead binding assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: In EOGT-deficient cells, the binding of JAG1 was not reduced.
source: In EOGT-deficient cells, the binding of DLL1 and DLL4, but not JAG1, canonical Notch ligands was reduced, and ligand-induced Notch signaling was impaired.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry and bead binding assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ligand-induced Notch signaling was impaired in EOGT-deficient cells.
source: In EOGT-deficient cells, the binding of DLL1 and DLL4, but not JAG1, canonical Notch ligands was reduced, and ligand-induced Notch signaling was impaired.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Notch signaling assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutagenesis of O-GlcNAc sites on NOTCH1 resulted in decreased binding of DLL4.
source: Mutagenesis of O-GlcNAc sites on NOTCH1 also resulted in decreased binding of DLL4.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from bead binding assays with NOTCH1 mutants shown in Figure 2.

claim: Global deletion of Eogt resulted in defective retinal angiogenesis.
source: Global or endothelial cell-specific deletion of Eogt resulted in defective retinal angiogenesis, with a mild phenotype similar to that caused by reduced Notch signaling in retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Endothelial cell-specific deletion of Eogt resulted in defective retinal angiogenesis.
source: Global or endothelial cell-specific deletion of Eogt resulted in defective retinal angiogenesis, with a mild phenotype similar to that caused by reduced Notch signaling in retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The retinal angiogenesis phenotype in Eogt-null mice is similar to that caused by reduced Notch signaling in retina.
source: Global or endothelial cell-specific deletion of Eogt resulted in defective retinal angiogenesis, with a mild phenotype similar to that caused by reduced Notch signaling in retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published literature on Notch pathway mutants and experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Combined deficiency of different Notch1 mutant alleles exacerbated the abnormalities in Eogt−/− retina.
source: Combined deficiency of different Notch1 mutant alleles exacerbated the abnormalities in Eogt−/− retina, and Notch target gene expression was decreased in Eogt−/−endothelial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from compound mutant retinal analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Notch target gene expression was decreased in Eogt−/− endothelial cells.
source: Combined deficiency of different Notch1 mutant alleles exacerbated the abnormalities in Eogt−/− retina, and Notch target gene expression was decreased in Eogt−/−endothelial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: O-GlcNAc on EGF repeats of Notch receptors mediates ligand-induced Notch signaling required in endothelial cells for optimal vascular development.
source: Thus, O-GlcNAc on EGF repeats of Notch receptors mediates ligand-induced Notch signaling required in endothelial cells for optimal vascular development.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: N-acetylglucosamine linked to Ser or Thr (O-GlcNAc) is a rare form of post-translational modification specifically modifying epidermal growth factor-like (EGF) domains in secreted or membrane proteins.
source: N-acetylglucosamine linked to Ser or Thr (O-GlcNAc) is a rare form of post-translational modification specifically modifying epidermal growth factor-like (EGF) domains in secreted or membrane proteins (Alfaro et al., 2012; Matsuura et al., 2008; Stanley and Okajima, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EGF-specific O-GlcNAcylation occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by the action of EOGT.
source: In contrast to O-GlcNAc modification of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins (Ma and Hart, 2014), EGF-specific O-GlcNAcylation occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by the action of the EGF-domain-specific O-GlcNAc transferase, EOGT (Sakaidani et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only a small number of secreted or membrane proteins have been shown to be O-GlcNAcylated, including Notch receptors and their ligands.
source: To date, only a small number of secreted or membrane proteins have been shown to be O-GlcNAcylated, including Notch receptors and their ligands (Alfaro et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2013; Tashima and Stanley, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Notch receptors are modified by O-fucose and O-glucose glycans at independent consensus sites on EGF repeats.
source: Notch receptors are also modified by O-fucose and O-glucose glycans at independent consensus sites on EGF repeats (Figure 1A), and both types of O-glycan regulate the strength of Notch signaling (Haltom and Jafar-Nejad, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Both O-fucose and O-glucose glycans regulate the strength of Notch signaling.
source: Notch receptors are also modified by O-fucose and O-glucose glycans at independent consensus sites on EGF repeats (Figure 1A), and both types of O-glycan regulate the strength of Notch signaling (Haltom and Jafar-Nejad, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of O-fucose glycans reduces binding of canonical Notch ligands to Notch receptors, and consequently Notch signaling.
source: Loss of O-fucose, but not O-glucose glycans reduces binding of canonical Notch ligands to Notch receptors, and consequently Notch signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss of O-glucose glycans does not reduce binding of canonical Notch ligands to Notch receptors.
source: Loss of O-fucose, but not O-glucose glycans reduces binding of canonical Notch ligands to Notch receptors, and consequently Notch signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Notch receptors lacking only O-GlcNAc glycans have reduced ligand-induced Notch signaling.
source: In this paper, we report that Notch receptors lacking only O-GlcNAc glycans have reduced ligand-induced Notch signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by experimental data in Figures 1-3.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations of EOGT and DOCK6 were identified as the basis of an autosomal-recessive form of AOS.
source: Among these, loss-of-function mutations of EOGT and DOCK6 were identified as the basis of an autosomal-recessive form of AOS (Shaheen et al., 2013, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Autosomal dominant mutations of NOTCH1, RBPJ, DLL4 and ARHGAP31 give rise to AOS.
source: In addition, autosomal dominant mutations of NOTCH1, RBPJ, DLL4 and ARHGAP31 give rise to AOS (Aminkeng, 2015; Hassed et al., 2012; Meester et al., 2015; Southgate et al., 2015; Stittrich et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Eogt transcripts were reduced by ~60% in Eogt-siRNA Lec1 cells.
source: Eogt transcripts determined by quantitative RT-PCR were reduced by ~60%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: Eogt-siRNA Lec1 cells exhibited reduced binding of soluble DLL1-Fc and DLL4-Fc.
source: Eogt-siRNA Lec1 cells exhibited reduced binding of soluble DLL1-Fc and DLL4-Fc (Figure 1B and Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Binding of soluble JAG1-Fc was not altered by knockdown of Eogt.
source: However, binding of soluble JAG1-Fc was not altered by knockdown of Eogt (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Overexpression of an EOGT cDNA rescued DLL1 and DLL4 binding in Eogt knockdown cells.
source: Overexpression of an EOGT cDNA rescued DLL1 and DLL4 binding (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cell surface expression of NOTCH1 was not reduced in Lec1 cells with reduced Eogt.
source: Moreover, cell surface expression of NOTCH1 was not reduced in Lec1 cells with reduced Eogt (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 1B.

claim: EOGT-null HEK293T cells exhibited decreased binding to DLL4 beads.
source: Similar to Eogt-siRNA CHO Lec1 cells, EOGT-null HEK293T cells exhibited decreased binding to DLL4 beads, but not to JAG1 beads (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from bead binding assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: EOGT-null HEK293T cells did not exhibit decreased binding to JAG1 beads.
source: Similar to Eogt-siRNA CHO Lec1 cells, EOGT-null HEK293T cells exhibited decreased binding to DLL4 beads, but not to JAG1 beads (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from bead binding assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Simultaneous expression of Notch1 and Eogt enhanced DLL4 bead binding in both HEK293T and EOGT-null cells.
source: Furthermore, simultaneous expression of Notch1 and Eogt enhanced DLL4 but not JAG1 bead binding, in both HEK293T and EOGT-null cells (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from bead binding assays shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: Simultaneous expression of Notch1 and Eogt did not enhance JAG1 bead binding.
source: Furthermore, simultaneous expression of Notch1 and Eogt enhanced DLL4 but not JAG1 bead binding, in both HEK293T and EOGT-null cells (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from bead binding assays shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: The synergistic effect of Notch1 and Eogt on DLL4 bead binding provides strong evidence that EOGT potentiates DLL4-NOTCH1 physical interactions.
source: The synergistic effect of Notch1 and Eogt on DLL4 bead binding provide strong evidence that EOGT potentiates DLL4-NOTCH1 physical interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: Neither Eogt overexpression nor EOGT loss affected cell surface NOTCH1 expression.
source: As observed in Lec1 CHO cells (Figure 1B), neither Eogt overexpression nor EOGT loss affected cell surface NOTCH1 expression (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 1H.

claim: EOGT is not required for NOTCH1 trafficking to the plasma membrane.
source: Thus, EOGT is not required for NOTCH1 trafficking to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing unchanged cell surface NOTCH1 expression in EOGT-deficient cells.

claim: O-GlcNAc consensus sites in mouse NOTCH1 are conserved among mouse, human, rat, Chinese hamster and zebrafish in EGF10, 14, 15, 17, 20, 23, 26, 27 and 29.
source: A relatively small number of the EGF domains in mouse NOTCH1 contain the consensus sequence C5XXG(Y/F)(T/S)GXXC6, and these are conserved among mouse, human, rat, Chinese hamster and zebrafish in EGF10, 14, 15, 17, 20, 23, 26, 27 and 29 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell surface expression of NOTCH1Δ4xO-GlcNAc mutant was indistinguishable from wild-type NOTCH1.
source: Cell surface expression of the NOTCH1 mutants was indistinguishable from wild-type NOTCH1 (Figure 2B), consistent with unchanged NOTCH1 cell surface expression in EOGT-null HEK293T cells (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of Notch1Δ4xO-GlcNAc in Eogt-transfected cells resulted in an ~80% decrease in O-GlcNAc immunostain signal.
source: Expression of Notch1Δ4xO-GlcNAc in Eogt-transfected cells resulted in an ~80% decrease in O-GlcNAc immunostain signal (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ala substitution in only EGF2 and 10 (Notch1Δ2xO-GlcNAc) removed ~60% of the O-GlcNAc signal in Eogt transfectants.
source: By contrast, Ala substitution in only EGF2 and 10 (Notch1Δ2xO-GlcNAc) removed ~60% of the signal in Eogt transfectants (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The number of DLL4 beads bound to NOTCH1Δ4xO-GlcNAc transfectants was significantly decreased relative to wild-type NOTCH1.
source: Moreover, the number of DLL4 beads bound to NOTCH1Δ4xO-GlcNAc transfectants was significantly decreased relative to wild-type NOTCH1 (Figure 2E), similar to the decrease observed in EOGT-null cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from bead binding assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: O-GlcNAc in EGF2, 10, 17 and/or 20 are important contributors to DLL4/NOTCH1 interactions.
source: This suggests that O-GlcNAc in EGF2, 10, 17 and/or 20 are important contributors to DLL4/NOTCH1 interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from bead binding assays with NOTCH1 mutants.

claim: The number of JAG1 beads bound to Notch1 transfectants was not reduced in Notch1Δ4xO-GlcNAc transfectants, irrespective of Eogt overexpression.
source: In contrast, the number of JAG1 beads bound to Notch1 transfectants was not reduced in Notch1Δ4xO-GlcNAc transfectants, irrespective of Eogt overexpression (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from bead binding assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: O-GlcNAc on NOTCH1 EGF2, 10, 17 and/or 20 selectively affect DLL4/NOTCH1 but not JAG1/NOTCH1 physical interactions.
source: These results provide strong evidence that O-GlcNAc on NOTCH1 EGF2, 10, 17 and/or 20 selectively affect DLL4/NOTCH1 but not JAG1/NOTCH1 physical interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from bead binding assays with NOTCH1 mutants.

claim: A limited number of sites are O-GlcNAcylated in NOTCH1.
source: The substantial decrease in O-GlcNAc signal following removal of only four of the nine potential O-GlcNAcylation sites, suggests that a limited number of sites are O-GlcNAcylated in NOTCH1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing decreased O-GlcNAc signal in NOTCH1 mutants.

claim: All four EOGT-targeted shRNA constructs specifically reduced NOTCH1 activation.
source: All four EOGT-targeted shRNA constructs specifically reduced NOTCH1 activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The TA197 and TA198 shRNAs exhibited marked loss of O-GlcNAc on species comigrating with NOTCH1.
source: The TA197 and TA198 shRNAs that were most effective at reducing NOTCH1 activation (Figure 3A), exhibited marked loss of O-GlcNAc on species comigrating with NOTCH1 (Figure 3B; the lower band of the O-GlcNAc-positive doublet).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Overexpression of EOGT increased the amount of activated NOTCH1 induced by D1/L cells in control HeLa cells.
source: Overexpression of EOGT increased the amount of activated NOTCH1 induced by D1/L cells in control HeLa cells, including in the presence of the GSI (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Partial rescue of EOGT knockdown by TA197 was achieved by a human EOGT cDNA.
source: Partial rescue of EOGT knockdown by TA197 (and TA198, not shown) was achieved by a human EOGT cDNA (Figure 3C, D; representative of three independent experiments).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Reduction of Eogt correlated with reduced Notch signaling in CHO Lec1 cells.
source: Ligand-induced Notch signaling was also investigated in CHO Lec1 Eogt-siRNA cells (Tashima and Stanley, 2014) using the NOTCH1 ICD-responsive TP1-luciferase reporter. Reduction of Eogt correlated with reduced Notch signaling (Figure 3E) and transfection of a human EOGT cDNA largely rescued signaling in the Eogt knockdown cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Transfection of a human EOGT cDNA largely rescued signaling in the Eogt knockdown CHO Lec1 cells.
source: Reduction of Eogt correlated with reduced Notch signaling (Figure 3E) and transfection of a human EOGT cDNA largely rescued signaling in the Eogt knockdown cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Eogt−/− mice were obtained at the expected Mendelian ratio of ~25%.
source: Eogt−/− mice were obtained at the expected Mendelian ratio of ~25% (total n = 244), and did not exhibit obvious abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse breeding.

claim: Eogt−/− mice did not exhibit obvious abnormalities.
source: Eogt−/− mice were obtained at the expected Mendelian ratio of ~25% (total n = 244), and did not exhibit obvious abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation of the mice.

claim: Eogt is highly expressed in endothelial cells.
source: Since Eogt is highly expressed in ECs, and retinal angiogenesis requires Notch signaling (Roca and Adams, 2007), we focused our analysis on angiogenesis and vessel formation in the postnatal mouse retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: Eogt is expressed in endothelial cells of retinal arteries, capillaries and veins at P5.
source: We now show by in situ hybridization that Eogt is expressed in endothelial cells (EC) of retinal arteries, capillaries and veins at P5, and mainly in arteries and veins at P15 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Eogt is expressed mainly in arteries and veins at P15.
source: We now show by in situ hybridization that Eogt is expressed in endothelial cells (EC) of retinal arteries, capillaries and veins at P5, and mainly in arteries and veins at P15 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4G.

claim: At the P5 vascular front, Eogt signal was apparent in tip cells.
source: At the P5 vascular front, Eogt signal was apparent in tip cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Vascular progression toward the periphery was delayed in P5 Eogt−/− retina.
source: Although a vascular plexus was formed in P5 Eogt−/− retina, vascular progression toward the periphery was delayed (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Vessel maturation measured by the association of blood vessels with mural cells was compromised in P5 Eogt−/− retinas.
source: Vessel maturation measured by the association of blood vessels with mural cells was compromised, as evident by the reduced length of αSMA-positive vessels in P5 Eogt−/− retinas (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The distribution of anti-NG2-positive pericytes was unaffected at P5 in Eogt−/− retinas.
source: However, the distribution of anti-NG2-positive pericytes was unaffected at P5 in Eogt−/− retinas (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown.

claim: The density and number of branch points were increased in P5 Eogt−/− retinas.
source: By contrast, the density and number of branch points were increased in P5 Eogt−/− retinas (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The number of filopodia was increased in P5 Eogt−/− retinas.
source: At the vascular front, the number of filopodia was also increased in P5 Eogt−/− retinas (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: An increase in vascular branching was observed in P15 Eogt−/− retinas.
source: An increase in vascular branching was also observed in P15 Eogt−/− retinas (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The phenotype exhibited by Eogt−/− retinas is similar to, although weaker than, that observed in retinas of Notch pathway mutants.
source: Moreover, the phenotype exhibited by Eogt−/− retinas is similar to, although weaker than, that observed in retinas of Notch pathway mutants (Benedito et al., 2009; Kofler et al., 2015; Phng and Gerhardt, 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison with published literature on Notch pathway mutants.

claim: Vessel branching was increased in Tek-Cre:EogtF/F retinas compared with control Tek-Cre retinas at both P5 and P15.
source: In both P5 and P15 retinas, vessel branching was increased in Tek-Cre:EogtF/F retinas compared with control Tek-Cre retinas (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: EOGT in ECs regulates vascular branching during retinal angiogenesis.
source: Therefore, EOGT in ECs regulates vascular branching during retinal angiogenesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from EC-specific Eogt knockout mice.

claim: Notch1 heterozygous retinas showed increased vessel branching at P5.
source: As expected from previous reports (Hellström et al., 2007; Kofler et al., 2015), Notch1 heterozygous retinas showed increased vessel branching at P5, and a higher number of filopodia (Figure 6A,B and C), similar to that observed in retinas of Eogt-null mice (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 6A, B, and C.

claim: Notch1 heterozygous retinas showed a higher number of filopodia.
source: As expected from previous reports (Hellström et al., 2007; Kofler et al., 2015), Notch1 heterozygous retinas showed increased vessel branching at P5, and a higher number of filopodia (Figure 6A,B and C), similar to that observed in retinas of Eogt-null mice (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 6A, B, and C.

claim: Vascular defects in Eogt−/−Notch1+/− compound mutant retinas were exaggerated compared to single mutants.
source: These phenotypes were exaggerated in an Eogt−/− background. Enhanced vascular defects in Eogt−/−Notch1+/− compound mutant retinas were also observed in P15 retinas (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Rbpj+/− retinas exhibited elevated vessel branching at P5.
source: Similar to Notch1 heterozygotes, Rbpj+/− retinas exhibited elevated vessel branching at P5, which was further enhanced in Eogt−/−Rbpj+/− compound mutant retinas (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Vessel branching was further enhanced in Eogt−/−Rbpj+/− compound mutant retinas compared to single mutants.
source: Similar to Notch1 heterozygotes, Rbpj+/− retinas exhibited elevated vessel branching at P5, which was further enhanced in Eogt−/−Rbpj+/− compound mutant retinas (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The addition of O-GlcNAc by EOGT is important in regulating the Notch signaling pathway.
source: The enhancement in the Eogt−/− retinal vascular phenotype in two different Notch1 hypomorphic backgrounds that do not themselves exhibit retinal defects, strongly suggests that the addition of O-GlcNAc by EOGT is important in regulating the Notch signaling pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from compound mutant retinal analysis.

claim: Eogt−/− retina exhibited diffuse fibrinogen staining outside blood vessels.
source: In contrast, Eogt−/− retina exhibited diffuse fibrinogen staining outside blood vessels, and prominent staining on vessel walls (Figure 7A and B), showing the leakage of plasma proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Sulfo-NHS-LC-biotin was occasionally detected in extravascular spaces in perfused Eogt−/− retinas.
source: In contrast, sulfo-NHS-LC-biotin was occasionally detected in extravascular spaces in perfused Eogt−/− retinas (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from perfusion assays shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Vascular integrity is partly impaired in the absence of Eogt.
source: Taken together, these data suggested a partly impaired vascular integrity in the absence of Eogt.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from fibrinogen staining and perfusion assays.

claim: The combined loss of Eogt and a single Notch1 allele in compound mutant Eogt−/−Notch1+/− retinas gave a synergistic increase in extravasation of sulfo-NHS-LC-biotin along vessels.
source: Importantly, the combined loss of Eogt and a single Notch1 allele in compound mutant Eogt−/−Notch1+/− retinas gave a synergistic increase in extravasation of sulfo-NHS-LC-biotin along vessels (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from perfusion assays shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The synergistic effect on extravasation was also observed in Eogt−/−Rbpj+/− retinas.
source: The synergistic effect was also observed in Eogt−/−Rbpj+/− retinas (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from perfusion assays shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Eogt interacts with the Notch signaling pathway, thereby affecting retinal vascular integrity.
source: These results suggest that Eogt interacts with the Notch signaling pathway, thereby affecting retinal vascular integrity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from compound mutant retinal analysis.

claim: αSMA staining revealed intact coverage of retinal arteries with VSMC in P15 Eogt−/− mice.
source: Unlike Notch3−/− retinas, αSMA staining revealed intact coverage of retinal arteries with VSMC in P15 Eogt−/− mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Apparently normal pericyte investment was observed in P15 Eogt−/− retinas.
source: Moreover, apparently normal pericyte investment was observed in P15 Eogt−/− retinas, regardless of the presence or absence of elevated fibrinogen staining (Figure 7F), suggesting that sufficient Notch activity is maintained in mural cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Sufficient Notch activity is maintained in mural cells in Eogt−/− retinas.
source: Moreover, apparently normal pericyte investment was observed in P15 Eogt−/− retinas, regardless of the presence or absence of elevated fibrinogen staining (Figure 7F), suggesting that sufficient Notch activity is maintained in mural cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing normal pericyte coverage.

claim: Inactivation of Eogt in ECs in P15 Tek-Cre:EogtF/F retinas showed aberrant fibrinogen staining and sulfo-NHS-LC-biotin extravasation.
source: In contrast, inactivation of Eogt in ECs in P15 Tek-Cre:EogtF/F retinas showed aberrant fibrinogen staining and sulfo-NHS-LC-biotin extravasation (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining and perfusion assays shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Eogt functions in ECs contribute to the integrity of retinal vessels by acting on Notch signaling activity.
source: Taken together, these results show that Eogt functions in ECs contribute to the integrity of retinal vessels by acting on Notch signaling activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from EC-specific Eogt knockout mice.

claim: Eogt−/− ECs showed reduced expression of Hes1 and Hey1.
source: Eogt−/− ECs showed reduced expression of Notch pathway targets (Shawber et al., 2003), including Hes1 and Hey1 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Dll4 expression was markedly decreased in Eogt−/− ECs.
source: In fact, Dll4 expression was markedly decreased in Eogt−/− ECs, whereas expression of Jag1 and Notch receptors was maintained (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Expression of Jag1 and Notch receptors was maintained in Eogt−/− ECs.
source: In fact, Dll4 expression was markedly decreased in Eogt−/− ECs, whereas expression of Jag1 and Notch receptors was maintained (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In Eogt−/− ECs, expression of Vegfr2 and Vegfr3 was slightly increased compared with wild-type ECs.
source: In Eogt−/− ECs, expression of Vegfr2 and Vegfr3, but not Vegfr1, was slightly increased compared with wild-type ECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Expression of Vegfr1 was not increased in Eogt−/− ECs.
source: In Eogt−/− ECs, expression of Vegfr2 and Vegfr3, but not Vegfr1, was slightly increased compared with wild-type ECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: N-cadherin expression was relatively decreased in Eogt−/− ECs.
source: Similarly, N-cadherin expression was relatively decreased in Eogt−/− ECs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: DLL4 failed to induce Hey1 and Hes1 expression in Eogt−/− ECs.
source: In contrast, DLL4 failed to induce Hey1 and Hes1 expression in Eogt−/− ECs, whereas JAG1 induced a robust induction of these genes (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: JAG1 induced a robust induction of Hey1 and Hes1 in Eogt−/− ECs.
source: In contrast, DLL4 failed to induce Hey1 and Hes1 expression in Eogt−/− ECs, whereas JAG1 induced a robust induction of these genes (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: EOGT acts as a positive regulator for DLL4-induced Notch signaling in EC cells.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that EOGT acts as a positive regulator for DLL4-induced Notch signaling in EC cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis of Notch target genes.

claim: Exogenously expressed DLL4 and JAG1 in EOGT-null cells were expressed at the cell surface similarly to control HEK293T cells.
source: Exogenously expressed DLL4 and JAG1 in EOGT-null cells were expressed at the cell surface similarly to control HEK293T cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Notch ligands are presented on the cell surface in the absence of EOGT.
source: Thus, Notch ligands are presented on the cell surface in the absence of EOGT.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing normal cell surface expression of ligands in EOGT-null cells.

claim: Both DLL4 and JAG1 lacking O-GlcNAc induced upregulation of Hey1 in WT ECs similarly to controls.
source: Both DLL4 and JAG1 lacking O-GlcNAc induced upregulation of Hey1 in WT ECs similarly to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Neither DLL4 nor JAG1 needs O-GlcNAc to induce Notch signaling.
source: Thus, neither ligand needs O-GlcNAc to induce Notch signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from co-culture assays.

claim: Co-culture of Eogt−/− ECs with JAG1 sending cells induced mouse Hey1 expression to a level comparable with wild-type ECs.
source: By contrast, co-culture of Eogt−/− ECs with JAG1 sending cells induced mouse Hey1 expression to a level comparable with wild-type ECs (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Notch receptors in Eogt-null cells responded similarly to controls to JAG1 sending cells.
source: Thus, Notch receptors in Eogt-null cells responded similarly to controls to JAG1 sending cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from co-culture assays.

claim: EOGT is dispensable for DLL4 and JAG1 as inducers of Notch signaling.
source: These results suggest that EOGT is dispensable for DLL4 and JAG1 as inducers of Notch signaling, and that O-GlcNAc on Notch receptors is required for optimal DLL- but not JAG-induced Notch activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from co-culture assays.

claim: O-GlcNAc on Notch receptors is required for optimal DLL-induced Notch activation.
source: These results suggest that EOGT is dispensable for DLL4 and JAG1 as inducers of Notch signaling, and that O-GlcNAc on Notch receptors is required for optimal DLL- but not JAG-induced Notch activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from co-culture assays.

claim: O-GlcNAc on Notch receptors is not required for JAG-induced Notch activation.
source: These results suggest that EOGT is dispensable for DLL4 and JAG1 as inducers of Notch signaling, and that O-GlcNAc on Notch receptors is required for optimal DLL- but not JAG-induced Notch activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from co-culture assays.

claim: O-GlcNAc on Notch EGF repeats is a functional modification of Notch receptors that regulates Notch signaling.
source: Here, we show that O-GlcNAc on Notch EGF repeats is a functional modification of Notch receptors that regulates Notch signaling and is required for optimal stimulation by DLL ligands.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: O-GlcNAc on Notch EGF repeats is required for optimal stimulation by DLL ligands.
source: Here, we show that O-GlcNAc on Notch EGF repeats is a functional modification of Notch receptors that regulates Notch signaling and is required for optimal stimulation by DLL ligands.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: DLL4 constitutes the critical Notch ligand in regulating angiogenesis and vascular development.
source: DLL4 constitutes the critical Notch ligand in regulating angiogenesis and vascular development (Benedito et al., 2009; Hellström et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: JAG1 antagonizes Notch signaling during vasculogenesis.
source: By contrast, JAG1 antagonizes Notch signaling during vasculogenesis (Benedito et al., 2009; Pedrosa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EOGT-catalyzed O-GlcNAc modification potentiates DLL1- and DLL4-mediated NOTCH1 signaling in co-culture assays.
source: We show here that EOGT-catalyzed O-GlcNAc modification potentiates DLL1- and DLL4-mediated NOTCH1 signaling in co-culture assays and is required in vivo during retinal angiogenesis and the maintenance of retinal vascular integrity in mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data from co-culture assays shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: EOGT-catalyzed O-GlcNAc modification is required in vivo during retinal angiogenesis in mice.
source: We show here that EOGT-catalyzed O-GlcNAc modification potentiates DLL1- and DLL4-mediated NOTCH1 signaling in co-culture assays and is required in vivo during retinal angiogenesis and the maintenance of retinal vascular integrity in mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: EOGT-catalyzed O-GlcNAc modification is required for the maintenance of retinal vascular integrity in mice.
source: We show here that EOGT-catalyzed O-GlcNAc modification potentiates DLL1- and DLL4-mediated NOTCH1 signaling in co-culture assays and is required in vivo during retinal angiogenesis and the maintenance of retinal vascular integrity in mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data from vascular integrity analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: O-GlcNAc on EGF repeats located outside the canonical ligand-binding region affects DLL4-NOTCH1 binding.
source: Site-directed mutagenesis of O-GlcNAc consensus sites in mouse NOTCH1 revealed that O-GlcNAc on EGF repeats located outside the canonical ligand-binding region affects DLL4-NOTCH1 binding.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mice lacking EOGT have impaired retinal vascular development, with a phenotype characteristic of Notch pathway deficiencies in retina.
source: Using retinal angiogenesis as a sensitive assay of Notch signaling in vivo (Roca and Adams, 2007), we show that mice lacking EOGT have impaired retinal vascular development, with a phenotype characteristic of Notch pathway deficiencies in retina (Benedito et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data from retinal angiogenesis analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Endothelial functions of EOGT are responsible for the retinal vascular phenotype.
source: Moreover, we show that endothelial functions of EOGT are responsible for the retinal vascular phenotype.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data from EC-specific Eogt knockout mice shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7.

claim: O-GlcNAc on the EGF repeats of Notch receptors is required for optimal Notch signaling in developing retina.
source: Thus, O-GlcNAc on the EGF repeats of Notch receptors is required for optimal Notch signaling in developing retina, and likely in other Notch-dependent processes in mammals.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: O-GlcNAc on the EGF repeats of Notch receptors is likely required for optimal Notch signaling in other Notch-dependent processes in mammals.
source: Thus, O-GlcNAc on the EGF repeats of Notch receptors is required for optimal Notch signaling in developing retina, and likely in other Notch-dependent processes in mammals.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other biological contexts.

claim: The ability of EOGT to potentiate Delta ligands is similar to that of Fringe.
source: The ability of EOGT to potentiate Delta ligands is similar to that of Fringe, a glycosyltransferase that transfers GlcNAc to O-fucose on Notch receptors (Brückner et al., 2000; Moloney et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a comparison with published literature on Fringe function.

claim: Lfng−/− mice exhibit enhanced sprouting and increased density of the vascular area in retinal angiogenesis.
source: Lfng−/− mice exhibit enhanced sprouting and increased density of the vascular area in retinal angiogenesis (Benedito et al., 2009), a similarly mild phenotype to that in Eogt−/− retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fringe and Eogt might play complementary functions during retinal angiogenesis.
source: Thus, Fringe and Eogt might play complementary functions during retinal angiogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on comparison of phenotypes.

claim: Mfng inhibits JAG1-Notch signaling.
source: However, Mfng inhibits JAG1-Notch signaling (Benedito et al., 2009), whereas we found no effect on JAG1-induced Notch signaling in assays using Eogt-deficient or Eogt-overexpressing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The distinct effects of the different GlcNAc modifications of Notch receptors indicate that EOGT and Fringe glycosyltransferases possess different physiological functions.
source: Thus, the distinct effects of the different GlcNAc modifications of Notch receptors indicate that EOGT and Fringe glycosyltransferases possess different physiological functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison of experimental findings with published literature.

claim: Eogt-null mice exhibit no obvious abnormality in the skeleton.
source: Indeed, we observed no obvious abnormality in the skeleton (data not shown) of Eogt-null mice, making them phenotypically distinguishable from Lfng−/− mice (Evrard et al., 1998; Zhang and Gridley, 1998).
evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown.

claim: The phenotypic similarity and genetic interaction between Eogt and Notch1 in retinas suggest that decreased Notch signaling caused by Eogt mutation is mediated by impaired O-GlcNAcylation of Notch1.
source: The phenotypic similarity and genetic interaction between Eogt and Notch1 in retinas suggest that decreased Notch signaling caused by Eogt mutation is mediated by impaired O-GlcNAcylation of Notch1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from compound mutant retinal analysis.

claim: All Notch receptors are potentially modified with O-GlcNAc.
source: In fact, all Notch receptors are potentially modified with O-GlcNAc and NOTCH2 was reported to be O-GlcNAcylated in mouse cerebrocortical tissue (Alfaro et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NOTCH2 was reported to be O-GlcNAcylated in mouse cerebrocortical tissue.
source: In fact, all Notch receptors are potentially modified with O-GlcNAc and NOTCH2 was reported to be O-GlcNAcylated in mouse cerebrocortical tissue (Alfaro et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The GlcNAc transferred by Fringe or EOGT can be extended with galactose.
source: The GlcNAc transferred by Fringe or EOGT can be extended with galactose (Chen et al., 2001; Sakaidani et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inactivation of galactosyltransferase B4galt1 in Lec20 CHO cells abrogated the effects of LFNG on Notch signaling.
source: Interestingly, inactivation of galactosyltransferase B4galt1 in Lec20 CHO cells abrogated the effects of LFNG on Notch signaling (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Embryos lacking B4galt1 exhibit subtle Notch signaling defects during somitogenesis.
source: Consistent with roles for galactose in Notch regulation, embryos lacking B4galt1 exhibit subtle Notch signaling defects during somitogenesis (Chen et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A Y/F/L residue at the −1 site is not absolutely required for O-GlcNAc modification.
source: In the course of preparation of this manuscript, a study in Drosophila Notch revealed that a Y/F/L residue at the −1 site is not absolutely required for the modification (Harvey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: C5XXGX(T/S)GX2-3C6 can be proposed as a broad consensus site for O-GlcNAcylation.
source: Therefore, C5XXGX(T/S)GX2-3C6 can be proposed as a broad consensus site.
evidence: This is a proposal based on recent findings in the literature.

claim: Five domains (EGF4, 11, 12, 14 and 20) out of 15 Drosophila Notch EGF repeats containing the C5XXG(Y/F)(T/S)GXXC6 consensus were found to be major O-GlcNAcylation sites in embryos.
source: Consistent with this view, five domains (EGF4, 11, 12, 14 and 20) out of 15 Drosophila Notch EGF repeats containing the C5XXG(Y/F)(T/S)GXXC6 consensus were found to be major O-GlcNAcylation sites in embryos (Harvey et al., 2016) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Drosophila Eogt mutants fail to display an obvious loss of Notch signaling phenotypes.
source: It is also noteworthy that Drosophila Eogt mutants fail to display an obvious loss of Notch signaling phenotypes (Müller et al., 2013; Sakaidani et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Notch pathway mutations were found to suppress the wing blistering phenotype in Eogt knockdown flies.
source: Nevertheless, Notch pathway mutations were found to suppress the wing blistering phenotype in Eogt knockdown flies (Müller et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Eogt may affect Notch signaling in a tissue-specific manner.
source: Thus, Eogt may affect Notch signaling in a tissue-specific manner.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on findings in Drosophila.

claim: O-GlcNAc consensus sites on EGF repeats are poorly conserved between Drosophila Notch and mammalian NOTCH1.
source: However, O-GlcNAc consensus sites on EGF repeats are poorly conserved between Drosophila Notch and mammalian NOTCH1.
evidence: This is an observation based on sequence comparison.

claim: The elongation of O-GlcNAc by galactose is not observed in Drosophila embryos.
source: Moreover, the elongation of O-GlcNAc by galactose is not observed in Drosophila embryos (Harvey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Each of the glycosyltransferases responsible for O-glycans may have different effects on Notch receptor functions.
source: The combined data on roles for O-glycans in Notch signaling suggest that each of the responsible glycosyltransferases may have different effects on Notch receptor functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison of different glycosyltransferases.

claim: POFUT1 and POGLUT1 regulate the strength of Notch activation.
source: Thus, POFUT1 (Ofut1 in Drosophila) and POGLUT1 (Rumi in Drosophila), which catalyze O-fucosylation and O-glucosylation, respectively, regulate the strength of Notch activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Genetic inactivation of Pofut1/ofut1 in Drosophila results in diminished ligand binding to Notch.
source: Genetic inactivation of Pofut1/ofut1 in Drosophila results in diminished ligand binding to Notch and Poglut1/rumi mutation results in impaired Notch processing (Haltom and Jafar-Nejad, 2015; Stanley and Okajima, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Poglut1/rumi mutation results in impaired Notch processing.
source: Genetic inactivation of Pofut1/ofut1 in Drosophila results in diminished ligand binding to Notch and Poglut1/rumi mutation results in impaired Notch processing (Haltom and Jafar-Nejad, 2015; Stanley and Okajima, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila, xylose on O-glucose negatively regulates Notch signaling by reducing cell surface expression of Notch.
source: In Drosophila, xylose on O-glucose negatively regulates Notch signaling by reducing cell surface expression of Notch (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The distinct effects of O-glycans on Notch receptors, coupled with differential expression of the relevant glycosyltransferases explain why different human diseases arise from mutation of POFUT1, LFNG and EOGT.
source: The distinct effects of O-glycans on Notch receptors, coupled with differential expression of the relevant glycosyltransferases explain why different human diseases arise from mutation of POFUT1 (Dowling-Degos disease), LFNG (Spondylocostal Dysostosis) and EOGT (AOS) (Basmanav et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison of different glycosyltransferases and their associated diseases.

claim: Eogt-null mice do not exhibit abnormalities predicted from the symptoms of AOS patients.
source: Unexpectedly, Eogt-null mice do not exhibit abnormalities predicted from the symptoms of AOS patients.
evidence: This is an observation based on phenotypic analysis of the mice.

claim: The vascular defects observed in Eogt−/− mice are consistent with the view that small-vessel vasculopathy may be a basis for pathologies in AOS.
source: However, the vascular defects observed in Eogt−/− mice are consistent with the view that small-vessel vasculopathy may be a basis for pathologies in AOS.
